name: Exenatide
route: Injection under the skin twice daily before meals (a weekly form is no longer sold)
status: FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes since 2005; Byetta and Bydureon BCise brands discontinued in 2024, generic twice-daily form remains
mechanism: Synthetic copy of a Gila monster venom peptide that activates GLP-1 receptors, raising insulin when glucose is high and slowing stomach emptying

article.summary: Exenatide was the first GLP-1 drug, approved in 2005 for type 2 diabetes. Its Byetta and Bydureon brands were discontinued in 2024, but a generic twice-daily version remains.
article.takeaway: Exenatide is a synthetic version of exendin-4, a peptide discovered in the venom of the Gila monster lizard that happens to activate the human GLP-1 receptor.[^1] As Byetta, it became the first GLP-1 receptor agonist approved in the US in 2005, paving the way for later drugs such as semaglutide. Its large heart-safety trial showed it was safe but did not prove a significant reduction in heart attacks and strokes.[^2] AstraZeneca stopped selling both brand-name forms in 2024; a **generic twice-daily injection** is still available for adults with type 2 diabetes.[^3][^4]
glance: Approved 2005 (Byetta), 2012 (Bydureon); brands discontinued 2024; generic twice-daily product available
Blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes
Injection under the skin within an hour before the morning and evening meals
DURATION trials, the 14,752-person EXSCEL outcomes trial, and studies in youth and Parkinson's disease

blocks.text: In 1992 researchers isolated exendin-4 from Gila monster venom and found it acts on the same receptor as GLP-1, the human gut hormone that boosts insulin after meals.[^1] Exenatide is the lab-made version. It shares only about half its amino acid sequence with human GLP-1, but that difference makes it resistant to DPP-4, the enzyme that destroys natural GLP-1 within minutes.

items: **Pancreas:** more insulin and less glucagon when blood sugar is high
**Stomach:** slower emptying, which blunts the sugar spike after meals
**Brain:** reduced appetite, which often brings modest weight loss

blocks.text: Exenatide is approved, with diet and exercise, to improve blood sugar in adults with type 2 diabetes.[^4] The weekly extended-release form (Bydureon BCise) had also been approved for children 10 and older, based on a 24-week trial in which HbA1c fell 0.36 points on exenatide while rising 0.49 points on placebo.[^5] It is not for type 1 diabetes, and it should not be combined with other exenatide products.

rows: Weekly form cut HbA1c 1.9 points vs 1.5 with twice-daily dosing over 30 weeks[^6]
Major cardiovascular events in 11.4% vs 12.2% on placebo; safe, but benefit not proven[^2]
No slowing of motor decline over 96 weeks compared with placebo[^7]

blocks.text: The twice-daily product starts at 5 mcg injected under the skin within 60 minutes before the morning and evening meals (or the two main meals, at least six hours apart). After a month the dose can rise to 10 mcg twice daily. It should not be injected after a meal.[^4]
Bydureon BCise, the once-weekly autoinjector, and Byetta were discontinued by AstraZeneca in October 2024 as a business decision.[^3] Some older references still describe weekly exenatide dosing.

items: **Common:** nausea (which usually eases over time), vomiting, diarrhea, jitteriness, dizziness, headache and indigestion
**Low blood sugar,** mainly when combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin
**Serious but rare:** pancreatitis, kidney injury from dehydration, gallbladder disease and severe allergic reactions
**Low platelets:** an immune reaction can cause dangerous bleeding; the drug must be stopped and never restarted
**Kidneys:** not recommended when kidney function is severely reduced[^4]

blocks.text: The weekly extended-release form carried a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents; the twice-daily product does not.

evidence.label: Strong for glucose control; heart benefit unproven
evidence.text: Exenatide's blood sugar effects are well established in randomized trials.[^6] Its large cardiovascular trial confirmed safety but narrowly missed showing benefit, and a phase 3 trial found no effect on Parkinson's disease progression.[^2][^7]

faq.q: Is it true exenatide comes from a lizard?
faq.a: Its design does. Exendin-4 was first found in Gila monster venom.[^1] The medicine is made synthetically in a lab, not extracted from animals.

faq.q: Can I still get Byetta or Bydureon?
faq.a: No. AstraZeneca discontinued both in October 2024.[^3] A generic twice-daily exenatide is available, and many people have moved to other GLP-1 drugs.

faq.q: Does exenatide help with Parkinson's disease?
faq.a: Early small studies raised hope, but a 96-week phase 3 trial found no difference from placebo in how fast symptoms progressed.[^7] It is not approved for Parkinson's disease.

faq.q: Why take it before meals instead of after?
faq.a: Its main job is blunting the blood sugar rise that follows eating, so it needs to be on board before food arrives. Injecting after a meal is not recommended.[^4]
